common_name: Prince of Orange Crocosmia (Vivid Red-Orange Speckled-Throat Montbretia)

planting.note: Divide corm chains in early spring before growth resumes, or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; this older Dutch-raised hybrid is grown for its heavily speckled throat rather than a solid flower color.

directions: Prince of Orange forms an upright clump of dark green, sword-shaped foliage and sends up arching stems carrying a long succession of red-orange flowers, each throat marked with fine burgundy speckling around a gold center that sets it apart from the more evenly colored blooms of many other crocosmia cultivars. It flowers over an unusually long window from midsummer into early fall and later forms notably large, ornamental seedpods that hold up well in dried arrangements. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in early spring, since crowded corms flower less freely over time. Grow in full sun and well-drained soil that does not stay wet in winter.

planting.note: Divide corm chains in early spring before growth resumes, or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; Vulcan is one of the Bressingham hybrids bred by Alan Bloom from a Crocosmia masoniorum x paniculata cross and was selected for a shorter habit than its sister cultivar Bressingham Blaze.

directions: Vulcan is a compact Bressingham hybrid crocosmia bred by Alan Bloom, chosen from the same masoniorum x paniculata cross that produced Bressingham Blaze but kept notably shorter for front-of-border and smaller-garden use. Bright, ripe-tomato-red flowers are held outward on branched stems above narrow, pleated foliage from mid to late summer, drawing hummingbirds throughout the bloom period. It is reliable and floriferous from year to year without becoming as aggressive a spreader as some older montbretia types. Grow in full sun with moderate summer moisture and divide overcrowded clumps every few years to keep flowering strong.

planting.note: Divide corm chains in early spring before growth resumes, or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; Red King was selected by British gardener John Fitt and has been in cultivation since the 1920s, making it one of the older named crocosmia cultivars still widely grown.

directions: Red King is a compact, clump-forming heirloom crocosmia dating to the 1920s, with upright lance-shaped foliage and dark, branching, arching stems that carry funnel-shaped red flowers with contrasting yellow-orange throats from midsummer into mid-autumn. Its long bloom season and shorter stature compared with taller crocosmia cultivars make it useful for the front of a mixed border as well as containers. Flowers draw hummingbirds and other pollinators and hold up well as cut flowers. Grow in full sun and well-drained soil, and lift and divide crowded clumps every three to four years to renew vigor.

planting.note: Divide corm chains in early spring before growth resumes, or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; Columbus is notable for its reddish-purple flower buds, which give a two-tone effect as they open to orange-yellow blooms.

directions: Columbus produces erect clumps of sword-shaped mid-green leaves topped by branched sprays of reddish-purple buds that open into orange-yellow, tubular flowers marked with a paler throat and a fine red ring in the center. The contrast between the dark unopened buds and the brighter open flowers gives the sprays a two-tone effect through their long midsummer-to-early-fall bloom season. It is a vigorous grower that multiplies readily into substantial clumps and attracts hummingbirds. Plant in full sun and well-drained soil, and divide every three to four years when clumps become crowded and flowering declines.

common_name: Aletroides Watsonia (Red Tubular Winter-Growing Bugle Lily)

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained, clay-tolerant soil in full sun; this winter-growing, summer-dormant Cape species should be kept dry once foliage yellows, since it is native to renosterveld clay slopes with wet winters and dry summers.

directions: Watsonia aletroides is unmistakable among the bugle lilies for its down-turned, narrow, tubular flowers in shades of red, salmon, and occasionally pale pink or white, carried in tidy rows along a slender, unbranched spike above short, sword-shaped leaves. Unlike the summer-growing watsonias more commonly offered in the trade, this Cape species grows through the cool, wet winter and goes dormant in summer, so its watering schedule should be reversed from typical garden bulbs. It tolerates heavy clay and considerable drought once dormant, and the tubular red flowers are a strong draw for hummingbirds and sunbirds alike. In Gulf Coast gardens, plant where winter drainage is good and withhold water entirely once the foliage begins to yellow in late spring.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in moist, well-drained sandy soil in full sun; this small Western Cape fynbos species is slow to multiply and may skip flowering in some years, so patience and undisturbed clumps give the best results.

directions: Watsonia coccinea is one of the smallest species in the genus, forming compact tufts of sword-shaped leaves only a few inches tall from which short spikes of bright to dull scarlet, purple, or translucent pink flowers emerge in late winter to spring. In its native fynbos habitat on moist sandstone flats it flowers most reliably after wildfire and can otherwise skip a season, a trait to expect in cultivation as well. Its diminutive scale suits rock gardens, raised beds, and containers where larger watsonias would overwhelm the space. Keep soil evenly moist through the winter-spring growing season and allow it to dry out somewhat as the foliage fades for summer.

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in acidic, well-drained sandy soil in full sun to bright light; this fynbos species is best suited to deep pots or raised beds where sandy, well-drained conditions can be maintained, and it needs heavy watering from autumn through late spring.

directions: Watsonia humilis is a diminutive Western Cape fynbos species forming short, congested flower spikes densely packed with relatively large blooms for the plant's small stature, opening over a two-to-three-week window in late spring. Its compact size makes it a good candidate for deep containers or rock garden pockets rather than open borders, where taller watsonias would crowd it out. It prefers a lean, acidic, sandy growing medium such as equal parts coarse sand and well-rotted compost, watered heavily during its autumn-to-spring growing season and kept drier once dormant in summer. Because it is uncommon and slow to establish, source corms only from reputable specialist growers rather than wild-collected stock.
